chapters.1.lds: Why does Paul place the hearers' need beside his own desire to depart?
chapters.1.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the saints at Philippi with their overseers and servants. Paul thanks God for their partnership from the first day. He prays that their love will grow in knowledge. He says his chains have helped the good news spread through the whole guard. Some announce Christ from envy, some from good will, and he rejoices. He does not know whether he will live or die. To live is Christ, and to die is gain. He asks them to stand firm in one spirit and not fear their opponents.
chapters.2.lds: The selected Church lesson teaches changed conduct through humility and care for others. How do Timothy and Epaphroditus give personal examples of concern for others?
chapters.2.summary: Paul asks them to be of one mind and to do nothing from rivalry. Each should count others better than himself. He tells them to have the mind of Christ Jesus. Christ existed in the form of God and emptied himself, taking a servant’s form. He was obedient to death on a cross. God exalted him, so that every knee will bow. They are to work out their salvation and shine as lights. Paul plans to send Timothy, and he sends back Epaphroditus, who nearly died.
chapters.3.lds: Why does Paul describe pursuit rather than claim completed perfection?
chapters.3.summary: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision. He lists his own grounds for confidence in the flesh. He was of Benjamin, a Pharisee, and blameless in the law. He counts all of it loss for the sake of knowing Christ. He wants a righteousness that is through faith. He has not yet reached the goal and presses on toward the prize. He asks them to follow his example. He says their citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will change their bodies.
chapters.4.lds: The selected Church lesson teaches joy and contentment through Christ during difficult conditions. How does the gift show that contentment can still welcome help?
chapters.4.summary: Paul begs Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord. He tells them to rejoice always and to bring every request to God. God’s peace will guard their hearts. They should think on what is true, honorable, just, pure, and lovely. Paul rejoices that they have renewed their care for him. He has learned to be content in plenty and in hunger. He thanks them for the gifts sent by Epaphroditus. He sends greetings, including from those of Caesar’s household.
